https://www.thetimes.com/culture/books/a.title: When I Grow Up: Conversations with Adults by Moya Sarner review
https://www.thetimes.com/culture/books/a.text:
Moya Sarner is beset by a gnawing doubt. She seems to be living an adult life — she ticks all the boxes, except for having a baby. Yet she feels increasingly that not “only did I not feel like an adult — I did not even know what one was.”
“What an adult is” turns out to be a very interesting question, and a surprisingly difficult one. Sarner’s approach in this thoughtful and painfully open book is journalistic: she asks a lot of people what they think. They range from psychologists and sociologists to people such as Boru, who survived addiction, and Sam, whose mother died when he was 13. Their stories are affecting and illustrate movingly how people grow up at different times and stages, from adolescence to old age by way of the midlife crisis (there are chapters for each phase). Sarner calls their formative experiences “grow-ups” and insists that they can happen at any age.
Her experts tend to agree. The neuroscientist Sarah-Jayne Blakemore observes that the brain does not enter some mature state, but develops “every time you have a new experience”. The literary theorist and psychoanalyst Josh Cohen suggests that an adult is someone “comfortable in the skin of his age”. The children’s author Jacqueline Wilson warns Sarner that adulthood isn’t “the pinnacle”, it is when “you start to pretend”. Rabbi Jeffrey Newman, who was arrested at an Extinction Rebellion protest at 77, talks about “learning more about living in the moment and discovering what it means to be of service” — growing up, in a way, even in your seventies.
Sarner learns to understand that adulthood is an attitude and a process, not something you acquire, like a dishwasher and 1.89 children. This conception is deeply informed by psychoanalysis — and while writing this book Sarner was training as a psychotherapist and undergoing analysis four times a week.
She talks about it, and her mental state, a lot. She describes having had a vision of herself as a wizened old tortoise beneath whose shell was “just darkness and some wisps of smoke”.
She sometimes seems on the verge of breaking down. Perhaps as a result, the goal of growing up increasingly blurs into achieving what you might call psychic wellness. For instance, Sarner feels “fireworks going off in my mind” when the psychoanalyst Margot Waddell tells her that a grown-up is someone “who can go on accepting their inadequacies”, and that growing up is “a process which with luck can be sustained”.
Sarner compiles an interesting portrait of adulthood, but there are gaps. She talks to lots of people, but not to the past, and not much to other cultures. She compares the Japanese respect for age with America’s obsession with youthfulness, for instance, and mentions that Chinese women seem to define adulthood more in terms of responsibility to others — but other non-western notions scarcely appear.
Nor does literature appear, apart from psychoanalytic literature and a couple of children’s authors. When in passing she mentions the bildungsroman, or coming-of-age novel, I found myself begging her to read one. Jane Austen has a few things to say on growing up. And what about Rudyard Kipling’s poem If? Generations have found in it the quintessential articulation of adulthood, admittedly of a masculine and stoical kind. And talking of stoics, how about the actual Stoics? But the philosophers seem to have been elbowed out by the psychoanalysts.
The other gap is awkwardly baby-shaped. Sarner says that she had hoped to be pregnant by the time she finished the book. And she admits that for many people becoming a parent equates with becoming an adult. Yet ultimately she dismisses this “seductive” idea as a lazy acceptance of a “linear” idea of adulthood.
I think this misrepresents what parents experience — and misses a central point about growing up. Being a parent doesn’t make you an adult, but it does tend to force or perhaps confirm a change in focus from yourself to someone else. I call that growing up. Psychoanalysis, with its relentless interiority, inevitably rejects such a view.
Sarner’s quest really set me thinking, but I struggle with the destination it arrived at. Adulthood means “to be as truthful to myself as I can to find out who I am and stick with me”? Grow up, I thought. And maybe dump the analyst.
When I Grow Up: Conversations with Adults in Search of Adulthood by Moya SarnerScribe £16.99 pp304

https://www.thetimes.com/life-style/sex-.title: Emma Thompson: why Iâm going naked at 63
https://www.thetimes.com/life-style/sex-.text:
âIâve never been to a sex party. Have you ever been to a sex party? Iâve never been invited to a sex party. Not once. Am I upset? Nooo. Hahahaha! Oh God, no.â
Dame Emma Thompson is sitting in her house in Scotland, clad in a jolly red Nordic jumper and red bobble hat with LED lights on it, eating a Rocky chocolate bar. (âI have to say, on first mouthful? Disappointing. This is a poor-quality chocolate bar.â) Her appearance leads me to believe that a) it is currently not quite as warm in Scotland as it is in London, and possibly b) that she also moonlights on the quiet helping Santa prepare wooden toys for boys and girls who have been good. Itâs a borderline Buddy the Elf look.
We were supposed to be doing this interview in London, but Thompson is having a difficult month â first, an old family friend in Scotland is dying, and she has cancelled all her current promo schedule, save this interview, to be with them. And then, yesterday, she fell over by a stream â âIt feels like a very 16th-century thing to be doing, falling over by a streamâ â and tore a ligament in her leg. Hence the current âmaximal cosyâ vibe of her rig-out, which complements her houseâs pine panelling, comfy sofa and lamp made from a very old, very corroded copper kettle with a glowing bulb inside (âGreg [her husband, the actor Greg Wise] made itâ), which appears to be the manifestation of Leonard Cohenâs Anthem (âForget your perfect offering/ Thereâs a crack in everything/ Thatâs how the light gets inâ) in a single accessory.
âYes! Very âhow the light gets inâ,â Thompson confirms, taking her second bite of the Rocky bar (âSecond bite: itâs becoming kind of all right nowâ).
The kettle, and the lyric, seem very apposite metaphors for what Thompson has spent the past 40 years doing: although sheâs played a range of characters in disparate projects, from Disney villain in Cruella to Elizabeth I in the sitcom Upstart Crow, one of her specialities is playing the light that shines through people when they crack. Often quite a painful, unbearable light: think of Miss Kenton in The Remains of the Day, desperately trying to hide her white-hot filament of longing for Anthony Hopkinsâ catastrophically repressed Stevens, or sensible Elinor Dashwood, weeping all the way through Hugh Grantâs unexpected yet longed-for marriage proposal in Sense and Sensibility.
Perhaps the most famous scene in her entire career is when Karen in Love Actually breaks down on realising that her husband, Alan Rickman, is having an affair. He gives her a CD instead of the gift-wrapped necklace she had earlier discovered in his coat pocket, which is clearly intended for another woman. As she palms the tears off her face and tries to calm her breathing before going back down to her family â so jolly! So capable! â she shows a marriage for what it is: the biggest emotional stakes most humans ever play for.
Itâs greater than any Marvel movie, where the whole Earth is in peril. Those films are like two-hour-long search beams. In Love Actually, itâs the tiny cracks of light in a middle-aged woman alone â her love bleeding out as she frantically remakes the marital bed â that still makes any audience gasp with her pain. I donât know anyone who isnât utterly destroyed by watching it. This scene is her Purple Rain, her Let It Be. Famously, technical difficulties meant she had to shoot it four times. Four times she gave that performance. How?
As she explained in an interview in 2018, âIâd had my heart broken very badly by Ken [Branagh, her husband at the time] â so I knew what it was like to find the necklace that wasnât meant for me.â In other words, that remembered pain was absolutely real.
Today, however â and please forgive the segue â weâre talking about very different kinds of cracks. Weâre talking about sex. SEX! Thompsonâs latest movie, Good Luck to You, Leo Grande, is one of those films likely to cross over from the film pages of newspapers to news and social media, as its topic presses any number of âIncoming Hot Take!â buttons. It centres on Nancy, played by Thompson â a repressed, dutiful, 55-year-old RE teacher who, despite a 30-year marriage and two children, has never had an orgasm. Now both widowed and retired, Nancy decides â in a moment where something, finally, cracks, and the light gets in â to have an adventure. She hires a hot young high-class escort, Leo Grande, to see if she can finally âsee what all the fuss is aboutâ.
The script takes on all the chunky issues around sex, sex work, ageing, power, class and feminism, while also providing lots of unexpected, tender backstory for what is essentially a deeply emotional, sexy and often very funny two-hander set in a mid-priced hotel room in Norwich.
However, the world being what it is, the headline news is that Dame Emma Thompson, now 63, has done not only a full-on, all positions, no-holds-barred explicit sex scene but also full-frontal, no-filter nudity. Tits, muff, the lot. Why?
âIâve never really been offered sex scenes,â Thompson says, pouring herself a cup of tea. âAs my mother said, Iâve basically played a series of âgoodâ women. I do âcerebralâ. And I have also never conformed to the shape or look of someone they might want to see naked. And by âtheyâ, I mean male executives. Iâm too mouthy, not pretty enough, not the right kind of body. And, crikey, you are constantly told what kind of body you have. In one interview I did, the male journalist wrote that Iâd put on a lot of weight since I appeared in Fortunes of War, and that my legs were ânow like tree trunksâ, and that Iâd âlet myself downâ. I was 31 and, quite frankly, no longer starving myself. I donât think anyone realises quite how thin most actresses are in real life. They look quiteâ¦ unreal.â
Itâs fascinating to note how Thompsonâs career is the inverse to that of most actresses. Usually, doing nude and sex scenes is the price young actresses have to pay to get their feet on the ladder â thankfully donning a cardigan as they hit middle-aged character roles, relieved never again to spend two days on a closed set, desperately negotiating just how much of their left tit will be visible on camera.
Thompson, on the other hand, seems to have waited until she had enough power and confidence to do sex and nudity in a way that matters. When, towards the end of the movie, Nancy finally stands, naked and postcoital, in front of a mirror and really looks at herself, itâs a moment as powerful as it is novel. To my knowledge, it is the first time we have ever seen on film an older, naked woman look at herself with simple joy. Such a tiny thing â but such a huge thing.
At the press conference for Good Luck to You, Leo Grande at the Berlin Biennale, the 30 seconds in which Thompson talked about this scene subsequently went viral on social media: âWomen have been brainwashed all our lives to hate our bodies â thatâs the fact of it,â she said, as a room full of seasoned hacks burst into spontaneous applause. She then stood up, away from the microphones, and shouted, âSo women, you try standing in front of a mirror, take your clothes off â and donât move. Just accept it, and donât judge it. Itâs the hardest thing Iâve ever had to do.â
âI canât do it,â Thompson says today. âNancy does something Iâve never done. When Iâm looking in the mirror, Iâm always trying to make myself look âbetterâ â turning this way or that, checking out my arse, pulling something in. Simply revealing my utter incapacity to accept my body as it is. But in the movie, at that point, Nancyâs body has just given her these seconds of pure pleasure and she is marvelling at it â not âitâ as it looks, but âitâ as it has become to her. A place she can be happy. A place she can find genuine bliss.â
As with most women, Thompsonâs relationship with her body is complex. While she might not be able to stand in front of a mirror without âjuggling it around a bitâ to make it more âacceptableâ, sheâs âpretty relaxedâ about nudity in general. âIâm totes relaxed in a communal changing room. There is something so relaxing about being in a room full of naked people â like in a German sauna. No one really takes any notice and most of us are just vaguely normal shapes â nothing stupendous, nothing grotesque.â
One of the pieces of preparation for the shooting of Leo Grande saw director Sophie Hyde get Thompson and co-star Daryl McCormack to lie on a huge sheet of paper, draw the outlines of their bodies and then pencil in arrows to various areas, writing their âstoriesâ next to them: the good and the bad. âWe had to write where weâd been hurt â both internal and external scars â and the bits we liked and didnât like. The bits I didnât like took some time, as you might imagine â I basically cross-hatched the whole f***ing thing â and then talked about what we did like. I chose my hands and my feet. I like my hands.â
Thompson holds them up â they look both elegant and hard-worked.
âDaryl took one of my hands and said, in this kind of wondering voice, âThe skin is very soft, and it moves about,â and I thought, âYep â because itâs 60 f***ing years old, thatâs why it happened. My cells stopped regenerating before you were born.â â
In a world where increasingly fewer women now keep their pubic hair â one US study revealed that 80 per cent choose to remove some or all of it â Thompsonâs revelation of her own pubic hair in the movie is also, madly, significant. âI had mine off too, for a bit, and am very cross, because it never grew back properly. I am older now, so itâs a bit pathetic and wispy. Iâd love to have a proper bush.â
Thompsonâs attitude to nudity (â âNudeâ is such a shit word, isnât it? Is ânakedâ better?â) is inherited from her parents, the actors Phyllida Law and the late Eric Thompson, who wrote and voiced The Magic Roundabout. âMy parents were very relaxed about it, which was regarded as weird by my schoolfriends but I learnt to ignore that because I thought it was stupid.â
Thompsonâs attitude to sex was informed by her parents too. She recalls that one of her earliest moments of, for want of a better term, sex education was hearing her parents having sex, clearly having âa wonderful timeâ. And Thompsonâs ability to find fun in sexuality can be seen in an anecdote she tells about when, as a teenager, she was preparing for a date and wrote a âto doâ list: â1) Wash and talc everywhere. 2) Pluck eyebrows. 3) Make-up. 4) Paint nails. 5) Shave legs.â
Her mother found the list and edited it, replacing all the key words with âbumâ so that when Thompson found it, the list now read, âWash and talc BUM, pluck BUM.â
Thompson continued this joyous vibe with her daughter, Gaia, now 21. âI wrote a booklet for Gaia about sex when she was little and, instead of âsexâ, I used the word âshavoomâ. I thought it was friendlier and fun. Itâs a hard word, sex. It has no softness, and so much of sex can be about softness.â
For someone starring in possibly the most sexually explicit movie of 2022, Thompsonâs own view on what she most values about sex is intriguingly at odds with her turn in Leo Grande. âFor me, sex is infinitely private. The privacy is what is so sacredly erotic.â
So, once again â why has she done it?----------There is one thing that perhaps has not occurred to Emma Thompsonâs detractors â and, despite the national treasure status, the Oscars, the decades-long charity work and the international recognition, she has them. She is regularly referred to as âluvvieâ, âmouthyâ, and The Daily Telegraph once asked, âIs this the most annoying woman in Britain?â (Amusingly, the piece actually concluded that she was pretty smashing but, still, the headline remains on Google.) And that thing is this: maybe sheâs not for you?
Maybe you donât need a liberal, humorous, intellectual feminist who is equally as likely to be on an Extinction Rebellion march as on the red carpet at Cannes. Maybe you didnât need to grow up seeing a woman who could both write and star in her own sketch show â 1988âs Thompson â but also turn her hand to high drama and Oscar-winning screenplays. Someone both incredibly socially and politically engaged, but also able to clown around with her comedy peers Robbie Coltrane, Ben Elton, Hugh Laurie and Stephen Fry in the TV sketch show Alfresco. A clever, witty woman who wasnât a train wreck or a hot mess just getting on with what she was obviously talented at.
For myself, growing up in the Eighties and Nineties, I know I needed her. My sisters and I worshipped Thompson â the largest picture on our bedroom wall, alongside Rik Mayall and Barbra Streisand and the Beastie Boys, was of Thompson. Back then, which other women were doing, well, everything?
In 2022, of course, there are now two whole generations of women successfully doing what Thompson alone was doing decades ago: her direct cultural descendants are powerhouses like Phoebe Waller-Bridge, Sharon Horgan, Lena Dunham and Michaela Coel â writers/actors who are equally capable of tackling serious issues as they are executing the perfect pratfall.
In these days of #MeToo and âfeministâ T-shirts in H&M, itâs hard to remember just how alone Thompson was, culturally, back then.
âI remember, during Alfresco, we [Thompson, Fry and Laurie] did a gig at the Birmingham Exhibition Centre. We were at the Philips Small Appliances campaign dinner and we went onâ¦ well, I was on after the stripper. She was giving a demonstration of the Philips Ladyshave, topless. I said to the boys, âIâm not doing this. We canât do this,â and they said, âBut Em, if we donât do it, we wonât get paid.â I just thought, well, weâve come all this way, Iâd better do it then. So I put on a huge tam-oâ-shanter and a long raincoat and sang a comic song about a Scottish castle to all these blokes in suits. And itâs not as if these things donât still happen â itâs like those sex parties in Silicon Valley where the women, if they go, theyâre sluts, and if they donât go, theyâre killjoys who donât get promoted. At least I donât get invited to them.â
Itâs this very clear-eyed knowledge of who has, and abuses, power that informs much of Thompsonâs life. She was one of the most high-profile people to speak out about Harvey Weinstein, giving a half-hour interview to Emily Maitlis on Newsnight in which she called him a âpredatorâ and a âbullyâ who was âthe tip of the icebergâ of harassment in Hollywood. She noted, âI spent my twenties trying to get old menâs tongues out of my mouth,â and added that sheâd threatened to walk from Brideshead Revisited when a male executive told a female co-star, Hayley Atwell, to lose weight. âI will always speak up because I am bolshy, and I will take someoneâs head off if I see anything like that.â
For some reason, itâs this bolshiness â whether talking about Weinstein or climate change â that seems to irritate Thompsonâs detractors. Why canât she just be one of Britainâs greatest actors and gracefully keep her mouth shut? Like lovely Dame Judi Dench. She never gets political. Or Dame Maggie Smith. So lovely. So quiet.
âThere seems to be this belief that you canât have or hold moral principles â ones youâve had for decades â if youâre also trotting up red carpets decked out like a Christmas f***ing pony,â Thompson says animatedly. âEither youâve got to go around in grey linen and speak about the horrors of the world, or you get into lots of sequins and tap-dance up that glittery rug â but you canât do both. And thatâs mad. Because human beings, apart from anything else, are so much more complicated and complex than that. We all are. I donât know why thereâs this resistance towards acknowledging weâre such a mixture. And besides, I canât just âpick oneâ â I donât have access to acting, that thing that I do, without the moral thing. It comes with it. I canât extricate it. The energy cells are weirdly connected.â
In what way?
âThe energy that comes from oneâs sort of perennial fury at whatâs done in the world â to women in particular, but all injustice. It informs my decisions and my writing and everything I do. Maybe it would be nice to ignore it. But for me, itâs just not possible.â
Hence getting her kit off for Leo Grande. âI knew I couldnât not do this movie,â she says firmly. âI knew it had to be made.â
Itâs important, she says, because â as one of the most successful actresses in the world â she knows exactly how difficult it is to get a movie made about any female character who isnât a sexy 25-year-old kung-fu scientist able to banter with her (10 years older, minimum) male co-star.
Before our interview, sheâd sent me an email detailing the kind of notes that female actors, writers and directors still get about their projects: âLove stories are weak.â âWe need more female characters â just change one of the men to a woman.â âYour female character canât cry â it makes her look weak.â That last note was, amazingly, about a character whose baby had just been kidnapped. A writer noted, âI feel like Iâm limited to the following descriptors for female characters: âbad-assâ, âsmart-assâ, âkick-assâ, âhard-assâ, âstrongâ, âtoughâ, âtough as nailsâ, âfierceâ or âfearlessâ.â
Male characters get to explore all their weaknesses â they get to be complex, deluded, unpleasant, sex-addicted, greedy. Complex. We get to see all their longings and wants. Thirty years ago, Richard Gere was able to hire sex worker Julia Roberts in Pretty Woman and it was just a delightful, aspirational rom-com. In 2022, Leo Grande sees a 55-year-old woman hire a young, hot sex worker for a single orgasm, and still the reviews have fretted over the morality of it.
âSurely weâre allowed to have one movie â just one! â where a woman wants something and does something men do all the time and we get to see what happens next. Donât we want to know what that story is? How it might change everyone involved?â
Including those who watch it: alongside women jubilant about Thompsonâs âlook in the mirrorâ moment, Thompson reports some of the most interesting reactions have been from male viewers, âyoung and old, having, maybe for the first time, conversations about female sexual pleasure. One older man said he saw the film and immediately went home and started to talk to his wife about what might give her pleasure. For the first time.â
This is the kind of film that starts conversations on a difficult topic. And it simply wouldnât have been made without Thompsonâs willingness to â whatever her own beliefs about sex and nudity â roll around in front of the cameras at 63 with her bra off.
Thompson has been a national treasure for more than four decades â first as a pioneer and now as an institution. I ask her what advice she gives other women in the industry. âBono from U2 has this thing called âthe Bono Talkâ,â I tell her. âHe warns upcoming bands about the pitfalls of fame, groupies and money. Do you have a Dame Emma Thompson Talk?â
âItâs interesting,â Thompson muses, diplomatically. âIâm sure Bono gives brilliant talks on how to cope with worldwide fame â but heâs probably talking to other men who are already in successful bands. For me, Iâm talking to women who are still struggling, who might be 40 and still trying to get their work in front of anyone and get something made. Itâs more, âLove, have you got a babysitter?â than, âDude, these limos are the best.â â
Itâs now getting late and so â having talked about sex, pubes, feminism, power, abuse and Birmingham â Dame Emma Thompson finally finishes her Rocky chocolate bar. âConclusion? Tolerable.â She says a cheerful âfarewellâ and goes off to jump in the cold stream outside. Because her leg still aches, and sometimes doing something that feels at first shocking and painful â and maybe initially unfathomable to other people â makes things better.Good Luck to You, Leo Grande is released in cinemas on June 17

https://www.thetimes.com/article/giving-.title: First they made their fortunes. Now they’re giving them away
https://www.thetimes.com/article/giving-.text:
The fashion industry is culpable for obscene amounts of environmental damage and the more I learn about its impact, the more I reflect on my part within it,” wrote Cara Delevingne as she launched her charity, Initiative Earth, with a £350,000 investment last year. “I am learning from my mistakes and I am dedicated to making informed decisions, as well as working with companies who are taking significant steps in reducing their impact.”
It was a moment of self-awareness and self-acceptance for the 29-year-old model and actress, who is determined to use a chunk of her £41 million fortune and her influence (she has 43 million followers on Instagram) to help protect the planet. She is not alone. Recent surveys suggest that global philanthropic spending to help halt climate change stands at less than one or two per cent of the total, but it is rising fast — and Rich List philanthropists are at the vanguard. The 21st edition of The Sunday Times Giving List tracks more eco-giving than any before it. Higher education continues to be the most popular cause, as it has for decades, but wealthy individuals are increasingly likely to tout their green credentials.
Some, such as the billionaire hedge funder Sir Chris Hohn, have been spending millions on the issue for years. Hohn tops the Giving List for the first time since 2010, with close to £350 million of charitable expenditure. He has spent £117 million in the past year on climate change-related causes — more than on any other cause — through his Children’s Investment Fund Foundation (CIFF).
In 2019 it emerged that Hohn was one of the leading donors to Extinction Rebellion, the climate campaign group, to which he gifted £50,000 personally, with a further £150,000 thought to have come through CIFF. “Humanity is aggressively destroying the world with climate change and there is an urgent need for us all to wake up to this fact,” he said at the time.
CIFF has £628 million of grant commitments on its books for combating climate change, but Hohn has said much more is required. “Less than 1 per cent of philanthropic money is going into climate change, of which half is in the US even though the US is only 20 per cent of global emissions, so we need to see a massive step up … we really need other philanthropists to come in and increase the effort.”
To this end CIFF teamed up with more than 30 foundations at the Climate Ambition Summit in December 2020 to invest $6 billion in climate solutions by 2025. Calling climate change “the defining issue of our generation”, Hohn is also making it central to his investment decisions. He has turned his laser focus on the role played by global finance in the climate crisis. In March he urged shareholders to vote against bank directors involved in “greenwashing” and who lobby against climate action.
Other climate activists on the Rich List include Johan Eliasch, the billionaire former chief executive of the sporting goods company Head, who has bought up swathes of the Amazon rainforest. Eliasch, who served as special representative for deforestation and clean energy during Gordon Brown’s premiership, has pumped £500 million into saving the Amazon over the past 20 years. Today he owns 400,000 acres of rainforest in Amazonas, northwest Brazil, an area that is home to about 50,000 people and is now protected from illegal logging and burning. “We live in a connected world,” Eliasch says. “If you cut down the rainforest, rain falls in the wrong places. That causes flooding and food and water security issues. Flooding causes migration of people, and migration causes conflict. It is cause and effect. We have about four billion years before the sun usurps planet Earth, so we have plenty of time left — let’s not ruin it.”
To that end the Duke and Duchess of Cambridge’s Earthshot Prize was launched in October 2020 to recognise and award 50 or more environmental projects with £1 million each over the next ten years. Scotland’s largest private landowner, the Danish billionaire Anders Povlsen, has reportedly provided £1 million to the fund.
The rise of green philanthropy has been years in the making, says Neil Heslop, the chief executive of the Charities Aid Foundation, our partner in producing the Giving List. “It is about money,” Heslop says, “but it is also about using the individual’s platform to exert influence. Who would have thought that a hedge fund manager like Chris Hohn would be one of the largest benefactors of Extinction Rebellion?”
Green initiatives have been popular in the celebrity world for decades. Sting launched the Rainforest Foundation with his wife, Trudie Styler, in 1989. The wealth of the former Police frontman is now valued at £320 million after the sale of his back catalogue to Universal Music Publishing Group. More recently the band Coldplay — whose combined fortune is £471 million — have focused on climate change. The band gifted £750,000 to ClientEarth, an environmental charity, and £900,000 to the Ocean Cleanup in the past year.
Delevingne’s Initiative Earth aims to lobby governments, repair damaged ecosystems and educate via festivals, conferences and courses. Other Rich Listers with a lower public profile but greater financial clout are also shifting the green dial — among them Lisbet Rausing and Peter Baldwin (part of the Rausing dynasty, worth £9.49 billion) through their Arcadia Fund; Alan Parker (worth £2.8 billion) through his Oak Foundation; and the Weston family (worth £13.5 billion) through the Garfield Weston Foundation.
Green issues aside, overall more than £2.4 billion was gifted by the 100 leading philanthropists in this year’s Rich List. Seven gave away more than £100 million in the past year, 38 gifted more than £10 million, while 95 were members of the £1 million donors club. More than £510 million has been given by Rich Listers to offset the impacts of Covid-19 since March 2020. In February Joanne Rowling thanked her readers after sales of her book The Ickabog raised millions for charities. The Harry Potter author said it was “one of the most meaningful experiences” of her career. Beneficiaries of the fund included the British Red Cross and the Disasters Emergency Committee.
Young black philanthropists have claimed three of the top dozen places in the 21st edition of the Giving List. Lewis Hamilton, the seven times Formula One world champion, Mo Salah, the Liverpool striker, and Stormzy, the rap star, all feature prominently among our ranking of the most generous billionaires and millionaires in Britain.
Hamilton, who has largely kept his philanthropy discreet to date, pledged £20 million in the past year to his new Mission 44 foundation, named after his race number. The only black driver in F1 history, Hamilton’s foundation aims to support and empower young people from under-represented groups and reduce opportunity gaps in education and employment.
Meanwhile, Salah donated £2.4 million to the National Cancer Institute in Cairo in 2019 after it was severely damaged by a car bomb. The star’s philanthropy is one of several interventions in his homeland.
Last summer Stormzy extended his black scholarship initiative at Cambridge University. Launched in 2018, the Stormzy Scholarships helped boost the number of black applicants to the university by more than 50 per cent, raising the black student population above 200 for the first time. In partnership with HSBC, there will be a further 30 scholarships over the next three years, worth £20,000 for each year of a three or four-year degree. The cost of the scheme will be at least £1.8 million, half of which we have ascribed to Stormzy as an example of a young philanthropist leveraging their influence to maximum effect.
Neil Heslop, the chief executive of CAF, which partners The Sunday Times in producing the Giving List, says: “It is no accident that young change-makers of colour are leveraging their positions against the backdrop of Black Lives Matter. It’s about the democratisation of their influence through power.”

https://www.thetimes.com/article/climate.title: Climate protesters who glue themselves to roads face a year in jail
https://www.thetimes.com/article/climate.subtitle: Patel cracks down on tactics designed to frustrate police
https://www.thetimes.com/article/climate.text:
Environmental protesters could be jailed for up to a year if they lock themselves to gates, glue themselves to roads or block oil depots, under plans in the Queen’s Speech today.
A new public order bill includes three new criminal offences intended to stop groups such as Extinction Rebellion, Insulate Britain and Just Stop Oil from causing serious disruption.
It will ban protesters from chaining, glueing or using other measures to attach themselves to buildings, objects or one another. It will also enable police to stop and search protesters without any grounds for suspicion.
Boris Johnson will announce the legislation as one of 38 new bills that he says will “get our country back on track” and help deal with the cost-of-living crisis and create a “high-wage, high-skill” economy.
The speech will include measures designed to capitalise on Britain’s departure from the European Union, including removing hundreds of pieces of EU law from the statute book and cutting regulations for small businesses. Other areas covered by reforms include gene editing, data protection and trade policy.
It will also include measures designed to shore up Johnson’s support on the right of the Conservative Party, including replacing the Human Rights Act with a British bill of rights that will enable the automatic deportation of foreign offenders.
Johnson will argue that the speech will provide a “long-term, sustainable solution” to the cost-of-living crisis by providing “high-wage, high-skilled jobs”. Tory MPs, including some cabinet ministers, have urged him to bring forward tax cuts in the face of soaring inflation.
Johnson said: “This Queen’s Speech will get our country back on track, and I will strive — and this government will strive — night and day to deliver it.
“Because in spite of everything we have been through, we are going to ensure that over the two years we have left in this parliament, we spend every second uniting and levelling up this country, exactly as we said we would.”
He added: “We will get the country through the aftershocks of Covid, just as we got through Covid, with every ounce of ingenuity and compassion and hard work. By urgently pressing on with our mission to create the high-wage, high-skilled jobs that will drive economic growth across our whole United Kingdom. That is the long-term, sustainable solution to ease the burden on families and businesses.”
The Public Order Act will make it a criminal offence for people to “lock on” or go equipped to “lock on” to buildings, objects or other protesters, using equipment such as padlocks, chains, glue and bamboo scaffolding structures. The offence will carry a six-month jail sentence or unlimited fine.
It will also create a criminal offence of “interfering with key national infrastructure” including airports, railways, printing presses and oil depots, with a maximum sentence of a year in jail and an unlimited fine. A third new offence will make it illegal to obstruct major transport works such as the HS2 rail link, which will be punishable by up to six months in prison.
The present patchwork of potential offences relating to public demonstration can make it difficult to prevent disruption.
The two statutes that usually relate to environmental protesters are the Public Order Act 1986 and the Highways Act 1980. Protesters can also be charged with criminal damage if the police take the view that they have harmed public or private property.
However, the existing statutes and criminal law are beset with difficulties. For example, the Highways Act has a lack of clarity over what actually qualifies as a highway.
Also the public order offences have to be balanced under human rights legislation that guarantees freedom of assembly and association. Article 11 of the Human Rights Act 1998 states that “everyone has the right to freedom of peaceful assembly and to freedom of association with others”.
However, the article’s provisions can be overridden “for the prevention of disorder or crime”.
The government will also push ahead with new orders that aim to tackle protesters who repeatedly cause disruption. The orders will ban people from attending protests or conducting “protest-related activities”, with the threat of almost a year in jail.
The new criminal orders — dubbed “Asbos for crusties” by Home Office insiders — would prevent habitual protesters travelling around the country to disrupt motorways, A-roads, places such as Parliament Square and other critical infrastructure.
Stop and search powers will be extended so the police can seize items relating to protests such as tubes of glue or padlocks “without suspicion”.
The new bill resurrects several measures that were removed from the Police, Crime, Sentencing and Courts Act earlier this year by the House of Lords. The measures were dropped to stop the crime-fighting legislation from collapsing.
Her Majesty may be the most notable absence from today’s Queen’s Speech but for many Tory MPs, fretting after last week’s local election results, there are other concerning omissions (writes Oliver Wright).
This Queen’s Speech, with its 38 bills, represents the last significant opportunity for the Conservatives to deliver meaningful legislative change that can be implemented before the next election.
While ministers have been talking up initiatives ranging from changes to planning law, repealing burdensome EU regulations and cracking down on disruptive eco-protests, the package due to be announced by the Prince of Wales feels slightly underwhelming.
Johnson’s intention is to sell it as a plan to get the country “back on track” by freeing the economy and creating “high-wage, high-skilled jobs that will drive economic growth across our whole United Kingdom”.
And yet there appear to be few measures that, in the short term at least, will deliver those kinds of results. Some, like the move to free insurance companies to invest in big infrastructure projects and set up a new infrastructure bank, should in the medium term help boost growth. Others, such as the so-called Brexit freedoms bill, should reduce some burdens on business — but there has been precious little detail yet.
Meanwhile, levelling up is a long-term challenge that is seen as rather nebulous by the electorate and whose results will only be apparent long after the ballots have been counted in 2024.
Overall the package, as announced so far, feels a little light on big transformative ideas to improve public services following the pandemic or tackle some of the systemic problems of productivity that have held back economic growth.
For Tory MPs looking nervously ahead to the next election, there will be a concern that this does not feel like an administration buzzing with new ideas. And time is running out.
Public orderThe government’s big push will be giving the police powers to tackle activists who use tactics such as locking or glueing themselves to buildings (writes Geraldine Scott, Political Reporter).
Post-Brexit changes So-called red tape left over in UK law after Brexit is set to be cut and a Brexit freedom bill will make it easier for ministers to scrap EU law without a vote in parliament.
Counter-state threats This would reform the Official Secrets Act and make it easier to prosecute and deport foreign agents.
EnergyBoris Johnson last month unveiled a new energy strategy; new laws would give legislative effect to the plans.
Levelling up and regeneration Michael Gove has promised to write a series of far-reaching targets for levelling up into law, which this will do.
Renters’ reform The 2019 Conservative manifesto promised stronger safeguards for tenants, who would be protected under new laws from “no-fault” evictions under section 21 orders.
Human rights Dominic Raab has suggested that he wants a British bill of rights to replace the Human Rights Act, which will mean the government can automatically deport serious foreign criminals.
Media Laws will allow the privatisation of Channel 4 to go ahead. Section 40 of the Crime and Courts Act — plans to force publishers to pay both sides’ costs in disputes — will be axed.
Railways The bill will set up and define the role of Great British Railways, the new state-owned company replacing Network Rail which will oversee the UK’s rail infrastructure.
Mental health Draft reforms will make it more difficult for people with learning disabilities and autism to be detained in hospital.
Conversion therapy A draft bill is also expected on banning conversion practices, but trans conversion therapy will not be included.
Economic crime Companies House could be handed new powers to crack down on people fraudulently registering companies, while the seizure of crypto-assets could also be allowed.
Minimum wage Following the P&O crisis, Grant Shapps said that he wanted to give ports the power to refuse access to ferry services that did not pay crews the national minimum wage.
Carried over Bills being carried over from the last session include the Online Safety Bill, a clampdown on puppy smuggling, laws concerning HS2 and aims to prevent curbs on free speech in universities.
• Bans on foie gras and fur imports, amid concerns that they would lead to a rebellion on the Conservative right.
• The Planning Bill led to a revolt by Tory MPs who said that a “mutant algorithm” would force houses on their constituencies. The remnants will be included in the levelling-up bill.
• Reforms of the judicial review process, in which individuals and organisations could fight official decisions in the courts, have been shelved.
• A Brexit bill which would have enabled the government to make unilateral changes to the Northern Ireland protocol. It is being held for now.

https://www.thetimes.com/life-style/prop.title: Are heat pumps worth it or just a lot of hot air?
https://www.thetimes.com/life-style/prop.text:
From the road there is little to differentiate the huge grey warehouse from the others on the Slough Trading Estate. Perhaps the fleet of garish vans in the car park — bright pink tentacles on a purple background — are a clue. Only upon stepping inside the vast hangar does it becomes clear this is not a usual factory.
Below the soaring corrugated ceiling sit a pair of detached houses. One, built in red brick, is a replica of a typical 1970s three-bedroom home. The second, rendered in white, is constructed in the style of a home from the early 2000s. These two houses are at the epicentre of a revolution in domestic heating.
Greg Jackson, chief executive and founder of Octopus Energy, bounds through the door of the white house. Outside — and even in the hangar — it is a chilly day. But inside this demonstration home the thermometer on the wall reads 22.5C. “It’s toasty warm,” beams Jackson, 50, sporting grey stubble and wearing a white V-neck T-shirt, blue jeans and scuffed brown shoes. “It’s almost too hot.”
These two homes represent environmentalists’ great hope for the decarbonisation of British domestic heating. They are both equipped with air-source heat pumps, devices that act like fridges in reverse, extracting warmth from the air and using it to heat radiators and water in the tank. This is a green, carbon-free way to heat the nation’s homes. As long as the electricity used to power the heat pumps is from a clean source, the only by-product is water.
By comparison, a gas boiler produces carbon dioxide every time it turns on. Some 80 per cent of the nation’s homes are heated using gas and every day 25 million boilers fire up, producing nearly a fifth of Britain’s greenhouse gas emissions. In its drive to net zero, the government has pledged to phase out the installation of all new gas boilers by 2035.
Heat pumps are environmentalists’ preferred choice to replace them. But they are not popular elsewhere. They are widely viewed as expensive, inefficient and suitable only for the most modern of houses. Only 30,000 are installed each year, compared with 1.7 million gas boilers.
And this is where Jackson comes in — to show that heat pumps are affordable and effective. “We are bringing heat pumps to the mass market,” he says. So why do they have such a bad reputation? “As a nation we have gone about this arse about tit. We have had large leaky homes doing this so far. Each of them have been bespoke jobs — and that is expensive.”
Jackson’s mission is to target properties where installing heat pumps can be done cheaply and quickly. “If you want to decarbonise Britain, then you have to go after the low-hanging fruit. And that is three or four-bed semis. If we can get heat pumps into homes built from the 1970s onwards — like these two houses we have built here — that represents 40 per cent of British homes. You do it well, you improve your processes. And as you improve the mass-market solutions, as you bring down the costs, you get better solutions for specialist needs as well. Then you can go after the more difficult homes.”
This is what Jackson has been telling ministers for months. His message has gained traction. Until now the cost of installing a heat pump has been in excess of £10,000. And because heat pumps work best in well-insulated houses, the quoted prices have often been much higher due to the need to bring energy efficiency up to scratch. Jackson persuaded Downing Street that by targeting modern, relatively well-insulated homes, and by streamlining the process, the cost could be far lower.
His team calculated that 17 per cent of the nation’s homes are suitable for a heat pump with no additional insulation work. For these homes, after streamlining the installation process, the cost could be brought down to less than £8,000. And another 50 per cent of homes could be fitted with just £500 of additional work such as minor insulation, replacing some of the piping, or installing a new water tank. All in all, 67 per cent of homes could be fitted with a heat pump for less than £8,500.
Still, that is far more than a gas combi boiler, which can be bought and installed for about £2,500. So — at Jackson’s urging — the government agreed to provide funding to make up the difference. On May 23 the government’s boiler upgrade scheme goes live. Householders can get a £5,000 voucher to put towards the cost of an air-source heat pump (or £6,000 towards the cost of a more expensive ground-source heat pump). Most homeowners will have to find just £3,500.
“We’ve now got to a position where we can install a heat pump at a cost that is genuinely comparable to a gas boiler,” Jackson says. “And then we will keep on bringing the cost down so eventually you don’t need the grant.”
There is a lot riding on Octopus being right. The government has backed heat pumps and is said to have written its heat and buildings strategy based on Jackson’s calculations. Jackson admits his company also has a lot riding on the outcomes.
“We have taken a leap of faith,” he says. “We have invested £10 million in this centre and we did that before the voucher scheme was agreed. This is the UK’s first heat pump R&D and training centre. We are taking responsibility. When people said there weren’t enough installers, we set out to train them — we’re going to train 1,000 engineers a year here. People say heat pumps are too expensive — we’ll make them cheaper.
“If we were a typical tech company growing up in another market, we’d be innovating in secret and then launching. But we have to innovate in public to drive change. So for the buildings strategy we shared an incredible amount of what would otherwise be confidential analysis, not only with the government, but a lot of other industry stakeholders too, to show how a heat pump-based system could be cheaper in hardware and running costs than anyone expected.”
The 1970s demo home was constructed in line with building regulations from the era. It features a copper-pipe plumbing system, a gas boiler in the hall and a water tank in the airing cupboard. The bathroom is kitted out with a retro peach porcelain suite bought on eBay; the curtains and furniture are of their era. The 2000s house is built of hollow timber-framed walls, featuring modern electrics and a combi boiler. Since the homes went up last year, engineers have been removing the gas boilers and installing new heat pumps. They do this again and again, speeding up each time. “It’s like an F1 pitstop team,” says Jackson, “you practise and practise.”
Throughout this vast centre, engineers are tinkering with pipes and tubes, taking apart boilers and heat pumps and putting them back together.
Outside the back door to the 2000s home, the heat pump is encased inside a refrigerated box. It is currently operating at minus 3C. “We’ve had it down to minus 17C,” Jackson says. “The efficiency goes down a bit but it works and it’s still far more efficient than a boiler.”
At the moment Octopus installs only heat pumps made by other companies — Vaillant, Baxi, Daikin and others. But Jackson says they can be made better and cheaper. “There’s enormous improvement to be made and that’s what we’re going after,” he says. “The Ford Model T was not the world’s first car. But it was the first affordable car and it changed society.”
Jackson’s message is getting through. Despite having done no marketing for its heat pumps, Octopus already has 15,000 customers on a waiting list for one.
A week later I am on my way to visit Jackson again, this time at his office on Oxford Street, central London. On the Tube, an advert catches my eye: “Gas is expensive. Wind is cheap. Let’s build more wind.” It carries Octopus Energy’s logo.
It is a simple message with a simple logic, but at the time of the worst energy crisis in a generation not everyone agrees. Instead of building wind farms at sea and carpeting the countryside with solar panels, the counter-argument goes, we should be focusing on energy security and shoring up supplies of gas and oil. This argument has gained traction recently on the Tory back benches and in newspaper leader columns, but Jackson has no patience for it. “Gas and oil got us into this crisis,” he says. “The solution is not more gas and oil.”
He has no private office of his own; he sits with the rest of his staff in the open-plan space. Despite employing 3,000 staff globally, up from 300 just three years ago, there’s no HR or IT department (he believes they do not make his tech-savvy staff happier or more productive).
Sporting another V-neck T-shirt, this time with a blue pullover, Jackson looks more like a Silicon Valley tech investor taking a punt with a new start-up than an energy titan. But his business, which he started in 2015, is now worth more than £4 billion. To put that into perspective, the British Gas owner, Centrica — the UK’s biggest gas provider and one of its biggest electricity suppliers — is worth just under £5 billion. Crucially, though, Jackson’s role extends far beyond that of a CEO. He is seen as one of the green movement’s most effective communicators. A regular on TV and radio, before select committees and in meetings with ministers, his message is cutting through.
“We’ve got to electrify society,” he says. Yet despite his role pushing the climate lobby’s message, Jackson does not even consider his fight to be predominantly about climate change. “This is not about net zero any more. This is about national security and energy costs. Putin wouldn’t have the funding or the leverage if it weren’t for our reliance on fossil fuels from Russia and around the world. If we can electrify society, then we can cut the cord to Russia.”
Jackson admits that in the short term, gas needs to play a role. Currently we are hugely reliant on it. In 2020 gas-fired power stations generated 36 per cent of our electricity, compared with 28 per cent for wind and solar, 16 per cent for nuclear and 15 per cent for other renewable sources, such as hydropower. “At the moment we need to do everything we can to get through the crisis,” he says. “Can we eke a bit more out of existing gas reserves? I mean, in the very short term, that’s fine.”
But the key problem right now is how to help customers survive. With energy bills having gone up 50 per cent on April 1, and another rise expected in October, he says an extension of financial support schemes will be required, along with a much greater focus on energy efficiency.
This all strikes a chord for Jackson. He grew up in Saltburn, near Middlesbrough, where his mother, Sheila, juggled bringing up three children with studying by day and working in a pub in the evenings. “My mum knew which reminder was the final one before the power got cut off,” he says. “And she knew how many days after that to send a post-dated cheque.” But it didn’t always work and the power sometimes went off.
“Energy is something we all have to use. The stress of not being able to pay for it is something that has stayed with me.” Last autumn, as the energy crisis began to spiral, Jackson gave up his £150,000 salary, cutting his pay to the minimum wage and donating the rest to the company’s staff welfare and customer financial assistance schemes. Although it is a rare gesture, it is one he can afford to make. Jackson has a 6 per cent stake in the company, making him — on paper — a very wealthy man, though he has never taken a bonus.
His girlfriend, Deborah Cohen, is the science editor at ITV News. He has two sons from previous relationships, Lucas, 15, and Zach, 5, who attend state schools in London.
As for his own education, Jackson dropped out of Huntcliff secondary school in Saltburn when he was 16. “I did a milk round in the morning and stayed up coding on the computer in the evenings — school was really a bit of an inconvenience in between.” He focused on teaching himself electronics and computing. “But very quickly I realised the pace of change was so fast that I really should have more education in a changing world.” He returned to school to do A-levels and earned a place at Pembroke College, Cambridge, where he studied economics.
His CV after university is a whirlwind. He worked at consumer goods giant Procter & Gamble before a series of business ventures: a mirror manufacturer; a direct-mail company; a peer-to-peer lending system. He even bought a coffee shop he liked to save it from closure. He then launched C360, an online customer-relationship platform, which was sold for £4.5 million, of which he took a 42.5 per cent share.
“The privilege I had when we’d sold the tech business was the chance to choose what sector to be in,” he says. “In energy, we can tackle climate change, we can bring costs down and we can help struggling families.”
So how much of this is actually about climate change? Although he joined Greenpeace at the age of 16, Jackson insists he does not “believe in sackcloth and ashes”. “The job of companies like ours is enabling people to live the life they want to live while doing less damage to the planet.” To that end, he says, once we’re through the current crisis, fossil fuels must be phased out rapidly. “We need to dramatically scale up our renewable generation to the point where we are only using gas to fill the gaps.” He says nuclear may continue to play a role, but he is sceptical at the cost and speed of production of new projects. The vast majority of British electricity, he says, will come from renewables. “And then we can start to turn off gas altogether. And broadly speaking, if we work at the right pace, that can be a 10 to 15-year process.”
So how do we do that? After all, renewable power has an Achilles’ heel — what do we do when the wind doesn’t blow and the sun doesn’t shine?
“There are two pathways,” Jackson says. “One is expensive — we use massive amounts of battery storage, massive amounts of new infrastructure to try and make renewables behave like fossil fuels. The alternative is much cheaper: use smart technology to optimise our big uses of electricity to work best with renewables.”
This, then, is the crux of Jackson’s crusade.
His empire is vast and growing. Octopus Energy Group includes a retail energy business serving 3.2 million customers, an electric car business that sells and leases vehicles, and an energy generation company that manages wind and solar power assets in eight countries. The whole operation is underpinned by a software program called Kraken, which uses algorithms to run energy trading and customer billing, and can match the price of electricity to the availability of wind and solar power.
Kraken allows Octopus to operate at a much lower price than its competitors by employing fewer back-office staff. It also provides an independent income stream of £70 million a year, having been licensed to E.on, EDF, Good Energy and big energy companies in Australia and Japan.
It is an incredibly hard time for the energy industry. Since last summer 29 UK energy companies have collapsed as the price of gas soared far higher than they are allowed to charge customers. Octopus has been buffered by the fact it buys gas months in advance. “The gas that we were supplying in April, when the price cap went up, we actually paid for last August,” Jackson says. Octopus is the only outfit charging a lower rate than the new price cap (£50 less — though only for existing customers), a fact that Jackson says is also made possible by the Kraken-enabled cheaper running costs.
His company is also protected by more than £1 billion of investment, including £480 million from Al Gore’s Generation Investment Management in November and £240 million from the Canadian Pensions Plan Investment Board in December. Octopus has never made a profit — but Jackson stresses that it takes time to build a business and its cumulative losses so far are less than £275 million. “We’ve received investments that vastly exceed the losses.”
So what is Octopus? An energy company, a tech company, or something else? “We’re really an energy transition company,” Jackson says. In 2017 MPs sniggered when he told them his ambition was to be the “Amazon of energy”. Now he says: “Uber might be a better comparison, because it’s about matching supply and demand in real time, with massive, massive data. At the moment our national grid is run like a minicab office. It’s a load of people with a computer in front of them and a phone and they literally dispatch power to where it’s needed. Instead, let’s build a system like Uber where you have a massive amount of data, machine learning and artificial intelligence that matches supply and demand in every location in real time.”
Such a system would be far cheaper, Jackson says. “With energy from fossil fuels, you always have to pay for the input. If it’s from gas, from coal, you have to pay for the gas and the coal. But with energy from renewables, you are not paying for that input — there is a near-zero marginal cost.”
Once you have paid for the infrastructure, there are few further costs. “What we need to do is use our renewables at the time when they are abundant and that way you’re benefiting from near-zero marginal cost energy. If we build a renewable system that enables us to optimise transport and heating against renewables, we will have built a cheaper system than we’ve ever had before.”
In Jackson’s vision, software will be used to take data from weather forecasts, energy abundance and household usage to work out the best time to switch on a house’s heat pump to make it cheaper. And the battery in an electric car can help, by using bidirectional charging to help power the house when it is not needed overnight.
“You plug your electric car in and say you want it to be charged to 80 per cent by the morning. The system will take power from the car when electricity is in demand and expensive and, when it is most abundant and cheapest, it will charge the car’s battery again. This is all done by the tech — you don’t even have to think about it.”
I point out that many people don’t have off-street parking, so can’t plug their car into their homes. Again, Jackson says that to rapidly achieve change, you first need to go after the low-hanging fruit. “About 72 per cent of homes have off-street parking. Among the ones who don’t, car ownership is lower. And of those who have a car and don’t have off-street parking, they are more likely to live in big cities and just use their car for occasional journeys.”
I suggest that this means it is the middle classes who will benefit first, but he says this is a London-centric attitude. “Policymakers, influential thinkers, business people and journalists are more likely to live in London and have a certain experience and project that experience,” he says. “If you live in Rugby, you might have to drive to a business park a few miles away to get to work. You don’t have the Tube. And you’re more likely to live in a three-bed semi than a flat.”He says the on-street offering will improve with time. “Already, if you’re on our Electric Juice Network, you can charge at a public charging point and it appears on your Octopus bill.”
These questions often crop up — and they are a bugbear for Jackson. “Often when we speak to people in energy, they say, ‘Oh, but what about X?’ My grandma got through the pandemic by staying in touch with her family on a cheap Android tablet. She’s 97 and living in sheltered accommodation. If, when the iPhone was invented, people had said, ‘Oh, but what about Greg’s 97-year-old gran? She won’t be able to use it’ — well, we would never have got the iPhone and we wouldn’t have got the Android and we would never have got all the accessibility that’s now built in but wasn’t there at the beginning.”
He pauses, before adding: “I say let’s solve the big problems first and then we’ll get to the small problems. That way we can transform the world.”

https://www.thetimes.com/culture/tv-radi.title: BBC climate editor’s family were on protest front lines
https://www.thetimes.com/culture/tv-radi.subtitle: Colleagues describe journalist as a campaigner

The BBC’s climate editor has been labelled a “campaigner” by colleagues after he was found in breach of editorial rules for the second time in less than six months.
Justin Rowlatt, the BBC’s first climate editor, was spoken to by executives after he reported misleading claims about extreme weather in a Panorama documentary last November.
An investigation by the BBC executive complaints unit (ECU) found that the programme wrongly stated that weather-related deaths were increasing and that Madagascar was on the brink of the world’s first climate-induced famine.
“The Justin Rowlatt stuff is grim. These are not ‘mistakes’; he’s a campaigner,” one BBC source said. Another person said, despite the ruling against Rowlatt, campaign-like reporting had become more permissible at the BBC amid the climate emergency.
Rowlatt, 55, has family members involved in climate-change activism. Cordelia Rowlatt, his sister, was fined for participating in an Insulate Britain protest on the M25 last year.
Bee Rowlatt, his wife, an author and former BBC journalist, has been present at Extinction Rebellion protests, including one in 2018 in which Oxford Circus was blocked on Black Friday.
“Best thing about #blackfriday is Extinction Rebellion bringing Oxford St to a halt,” she tweeted next to a picture of protesters holding a banner reading “Rebel for life”.
In 2019 she called a pregnant activist who chained herself to a protester in central London “amazing”. The pregnant woman was unshackled by police and arrested.
Bee Rowlatt supported an Extinction Rebellion “justice” fund that gave protesters access to legal advice after they were charged. The fund raised more than £440,000.
She had a 20-year BBC career and appeared with Justin in the 2013 documentary Make Me a German, in which they travelled to Nuremberg to adopt a German lifestyle. Justin also documented family life for “Ethical Man”, a Newsnight project in which he set out to cut his household carbon emissions.
Ruling on Justin Rowlatt’s Panorama film, the BBC’s complaints unit noted that extreme weather deaths had decreased in number because of improved warning systems and disaster management. The unit said the documentary also said “without qualification” that Madagascar was close to the world’s first climate-induced famine.
The unit concluded last December that he gave an “inaccurate” impression of wind farm subsidies. He said in a report last June that the offshore wind industry was “now virtually subsidy-free”, when that statement applied only to recently approved projects.
The BBC said: “The views of BBC journalists’ family members are completely irrelevant to BBC editorial decisions, and we’re surprised The Times is suggesting otherwise. To conflate family members’ views with decisions made by the BBC’s ECU is quite simply poor journalism.”
